source.version_note: Frontiers in Psychology 14:1107306, published 9 March 2023; accepted 20 February 2023.
source.verification_method: All eight supplied pages read, including scale, fixed presentation order, example dilemma, statistical results, limitations and references.

citation.title: How automation level influences moral decisions of humans collaborating with industrial robots in different scenarios

reading.source_scope_note: Online responses to eight fixed-order hypothetical industrial dilemmas, not actual robot collaboration. Death/injury and interaction-level labels are confounded with individual story content. Terror management, rational adaptation and responsibility shift are explanations rather than directly measured mechanisms.
access_limits: All eight pages read; the supplied example is inspected in full. Supplementary Appendix A with all dilemmas and correlations is not embedded in this PDF.
Raw data, analysis code, full scenario texts, precise recoding and original ANOVA output were not independently inspected. Cited primary terror-management and automation studies remain unread.

study.sample: 265 start, 223 complete, one unspecified outlier excluded, final N=222. University mailing list/SurveyCircle recruitment, mean age 26.31, 56 men and approximately 75% women; predominantly student/higher-education context.
study.design: 2 dilemma types (death/injury) by four described human–robot interaction levels, all within person. Exactly one unique dilemma per cell, eight total. Scenarios appear in increasing interaction order, not randomized.
study.interaction_levels: Separate tasks/zones; shared task/cooperation zone; handover in shared workspace; direct physical joint task. Task, cause of malfunction, physical contact and implied autonomy vary together.
study.measurement: Four-point yes/no action tendency, reversed as needed to 1 deontological–4 utilitarian. Five-point retrospective confidence collected after all dilemmas; confidence outcomes not developed in the reported results. No actual action, advice uptake, responsibility or emotion measure.
study.results: More utilitarian-coded responses for injury than death, F(1,220)=150.51, partial eta-squared=.41; reported interaction-level main effect F(1,220)=65.86, eta=.23. Levels 2/3 do not differ. Interaction F(1,221)=23.26 is printed with eta=.95, which does not reconcile with the printed F/df.
study.interpretation: Observed differences among particular fixed stories do not independently establish a causal effect of proximity, automation, emotion, rationality, trust or accountability transfer. Authors acknowledge one-dilemma-per-cell and order limitations.

summary: Add terror management as an explicitly secondary theoretical account, not a demonstrated mechanism. Refine existing dual-process, psychological-distance and responsibility concepts using the study's substantial stimulus/order limits. No new proximity-induced-utilitarianism syndrome is created.

findings.definition: Responses to mortality-related anxiety that seek security in cultural beliefs and symbolic sources of stability.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary theory used to motivate a hypothesis; no mortality-salience manipulation, anxiety measure or direct test of the theory in this study
findings.ai_proposal: Study whether mortality-related framing in an AI-mediated discussion changes people's reliance on familiar norms or sources of security, using ethical consent and direct measures. Distinguish evidence-based caution from fear-driven rigidity; do not infer that a model experiences death anxiety or treats shutdown as human mortality.
findings.novelty_rationale: A particular theoretical account of responses to mortality awareness, distinct from generic emotion regulation, experiential avoidance, identity concerns or fear inferred from any safety choice. The source explicitly names and explains the theory rather than merely listing it.

findings.evidence_scope: Background describes terror-management theory and hypothesizes that death-related dilemmas may increase reliance on a familiar do-not-kill rule. The experiment does not separately manipulate mortality salience or measure anxiety, cultural worldview defense or self-esteem. Greenberg/Solomon/Pyszczynski's full original work remains unread.
findings.boundary: Mortality-related content, anxiety, cultural commitment and actual ethical correctness are distinct. Strong norms can be justified without fear, and fear need not cause a particular moral answer. This is a theoretical human process, not an AI diagnosis, universal motive or demonstrated explanation of this experiment.

findings.definition: Moral answers are coded along a deontological–utilitarian scale, but this coding does not establish automatic emotion versus effortful reasoning.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing theory and measurement boundary; do not add a new rationality-adaptation process from response direction alone.

findings.evidence_scope: The article explicitly introduces a dual-process account and acknowledges limits of inference from dilemma choices. It collects no response-time, process tracing, emotion, neural or strategy measure capable of discriminating its proposed processes.
findings.boundary: Utilitarian answers need not be unemotional, superior or slow; deontological answers need not be automatic, inflexible or irrational. A theoretical correspondence is not a one-to-one diagnostic mapping or evidence a robot has the same cognitive/affective processes.

findings.novelty_rationale: Clarify the existing subjective-distance concept rather than declare four physical task arrangements four levels of one psychological mechanism.

findings.evidence_scope: Workspace/task/contact descriptions vary alongside autonomy and story content. No direct subjective-distance or perceived-autonomy check establishes the intended psychological state.
findings.boundary: Physical distance, task interdependence, perceived intelligence, agency and subjective closeness are not synonyms. A pattern across fixed vignettes cannot uniquely identify any one of these causes. This boundary note is not a direct psychological-distance paper.

findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility-displacement concern; do not manufacture another direct source from an unmeasured explanation in the abstract.

findings.evidence_scope: The paper speculates about overreliance, lower emotional involvement and transferred responsibility, then proposes training. No responsibility, trust, disclosure, accountability or training outcome is measured.
findings.boundary: A more utilitarian-coded answer does not prove abdication, reduced responsibility or unwarranted reliance. Operational accountability also includes designers/institutions, not automatically every duty assigned to a human operator. Training efficacy and real risk reduction remain untested.

methodological_limits: This is a questionnaire about imagined workplace scenarios, not observed collaboration with a robot or an actual manipulation of its automation. All results concern stated action tendencies.

There is exactly one story per dilemma-type-by-level cell, so experimental factors are confounded with story-specific content, causal structure and required action. More people do not remove this stimulus-sampling problem.

Scenarios are always shown in increasing interaction level. Practice, anchoring, habituation, fatigue and perceived study purpose can covary with level. No feedback is needed for order/carryover effects to occur.

Task, physical contact, shared responsibility language, machine movement and implied autonomy change together. The design does not isolate proximity or demonstrate that all four descriptions differ as intended in subjective closeness.

The example death scenario requires pushing an uninvolved colleague as a physical barrier; other cells concern holding/lowering components or unspecified erratic motion. Means-versus-side-effect, physical agency and causal intelligibility can change independently of proximity.

Death and injury vignettes are different stories, not a single incident with severity alone changed. More utilitarian-coded injury responses cannot uniquely identify terror management, reduced emotion or a loss-risk theory.

A four-category ordinal yes/no response is described as continuous and as measuring hesitation, but can also express preference strength. Reversing scores to 1–4 does not create an independent interval-scaled measure of a person's moral philosophy.

Response direction does not establish rationality, correctness, cognitive effort or absence of affect. The article's strong System-1/deontology and System-2/utilitarianism mapping goes beyond what choices alone identify.

For a four-level factor and its interaction, numerator df=1 requires clarification of a trend or sphericity correction, which is not stated with the results. Printed denominator df alternate 220/221 despite N=222. Original analysis/sample handling is needed; no corrected df are guessed.

The interaction is reported F(1,221)=23.26 with partial eta-squared=.95. Under the printed F/df the ordinary partial eta-squared calculation is about .095, not .95. The printed p=.001 also needs original output; do not silently replace the reported result.

Level 2 versus level 3 is undetected, so the result is not a strictly increasing effect at every successive level. The interaction indicates different patterns for death and injury, further limiting a uniform main-effect story.

An outlier is excluded without sufficient criterion detail here. A priori power analysis is not presented despite claims of sufficient/high power. Sample size alone does not validate the stimuli, mechanism or exact magnitude.

Most inter-dilemma correlations are undetected, and the authors acknowledge that internal consistency/content validation are not established. A common 1–4 coding does not prove one reliable underlying trait.
Confidence is collected retrospectively after all dilemmas and no relevant confidence analysis is reported. Do not infer well-calibrated confidence or a measured confidence-based mechanism.

No direct measurements of robot trust, overreliance, emotion, responsibility, mortality anxiety or subjective autonomy establish the suggested explanations. Mortality salience is not an alias for terror-management responses or directly tested here.

A young, predominantly female/student, self-selected sample is not an industrial workforce or all robot users. The authors' educational-development explanation is a hypothesis, not proof that less educated people have inferior moral judgment.
An anonymous online format can reduce some audience pressure but does not guarantee no demand characteristics, impression management or hypothetical-versus-real action gap.

Physical separation and slow movement can support safety but do not literally guarantee all safety outcomes. Human responsibility language does not remove institutional duties or establish current legal accountability. No training intervention or actual incident prevention is evaluated.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Both sources interpret moral response changes through cognitive/affective accounts. Even actual fNIRS does not uniquely identify emotion regulation; this questionnaire has still less direct process evidence.

The rescue study separates two active choices and tests culpability. Its caveat against equating non-utilitarian choices with inaction applies here, where pushing a person and handling a component vary across stories.

Operational responsibility needs realistic authority and intervention capability. The statement ultimate responsibility rests with the human is not sufficient evidence that a particular worker is culpable or that a responsibility shift occurred.

Graphical risk allocation, fixed-order workplace stories and real human–robot behavior are different tasks. More lifelike wording does not establish external validity or a general reduction of self-protection.

deferred.reason: Descriptive label for responses across unique fixed-order stories; proximity and mechanism are not isolated, so no new independently identified behavior is added.
Related input/awareness construct, but not independently operationalized in this study. Keep it distinct from the theoretical terror-management response rather than add an unsupported exact synonym.
Speculative explanation inferred from utilitarian-coded answers; actual rationality, cognitive imitation or a unique adaptation process is not measured.
Already covered by existing responsibility concepts, and no direct responsibility measure or actual delegation is collected here.

limitations: One explicitly theoretical human concept added; existing mechanism notes remain scoped. No automatic violation/harm edges, actual safety improvement or machine emotion is inferred.
